source.anchor: Why do atoms form chemical bonds?

en.stem: Which reason best explains why two atoms may form a chemical bond?
en.answer: The bonded arrangement can have lower energy than the separate atoms.

options.text: Bonding always adds an electron to each nucleus.
The bonded arrangement can have lower energy than the separate atoms.
All atoms must become positively charged.
Bonding removes every electron from both atoms.

source.anchor: Why do atoms form chemical bonds?

en.stem: Explain how a more stable electron arrangement can favour chemical bonding.
en.answer: When atoms bond they can reach a lower-energy, more stable arrangement of electrons; the bonding interaction is favourable when its formation lowers the overall energy.

en.stem: Why are atoms with complete outer electron shells often less reactive than atoms with incomplete shells?
en.answer: A filled valence shell is relatively stable; such atoms have less tendency to gain, lose or share electrons to reach a stable configuration.

en.stem: Compare the electron movement in the formation of sodium chloride and a hydrogen molecule.

en.stem: Explain ionic and coordinate covalent bond formation using electron transfer and electron-pair donation.
en.answer: Ionic bond: one atom transfers electron(s) to another, giving oppositely charged ions whose electrostatic attraction holds them together (2 marks). Coordinate covalent bond: a shared pair is supplied initially by one donor atom to an electron-pair acceptor (2 marks). Explain that the coordinate bond behaves as a covalent bond once formed (1 mark).

en.stem: Relate metallic bonding to electrical conduction and the ability of metals to be shaped.

source.anchor: Compare the properties of ionic and covalent compounds

en.stem: Compare a typical ionic compound and a simple molecular covalent compound in bonding, melting behaviour and electrical conduction.
en.answer: Ionic compound: electrostatic attraction among cations/anions (1), usually higher melting point due to strong lattice forces (1), molten or dissolved state can conduct through mobile ions (1). Simple molecular covalent compound: atoms share electrons (1); it usually has weaker intermolecular attractions and is a poor electrical conductor because it lacks mobile charged particles (1).

en.answer: The O–H bond is an intramolecular covalent bond formed by sharing electrons; a hydrogen bond is an intermolecular attraction between suitable polar molecules.

en.stem: Explain why water can have a higher boiling point than a similar small molecular hydride that cannot form strong hydrogen bonds.
en.answer: Water has polar O–H bonds (1) and forms a network of intermolecular hydrogen bonds (2). More energy is needed to overcome these attractions when liquid water vaporises (1), raising its boiling point relative to a comparable hydride with weaker attractions (1).

en.stem: Explain how the bonding arrangement of graphite differs from that of diamond in a way that affects conductivity.
en.answer: Graphite has layers containing electrons that can move within the sheets, allowing conduction; diamond forms a three-dimensional covalent network in which bonding electrons are localised, so diamond does not normally conduct.

en.stem: Explain why an ionic crystal is often brittle when stress shifts its layers.
en.answer: A shift can bring ions of the same charge opposite one another; strong repulsion then causes the lattice to fracture instead of deforming plastically.
